en: Compiled by Master Daoyuan, Part 40:
The Meaning of the Five Lower Fetters (Part 5 of 5). Regarding the meaning of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):
the first is called sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); the second is called ill will (*vyāpāda*); the third is called the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The fourth is called adherence to precepts and vows;
the fifth is called doubt.
As for the craving of the desire realm, it covets the five external sensual desires.
Therefore, it is called "desire" (*rāga*).
Alternatively, because the desirous mind longs for a preceding object,
it is called "desire."
Anger toward an adverse object is termed hatred;
the perception of a self within the body is [the view of a self-identity].
It is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Taking precepts as the path is therefore called the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
In reality, one also takes giving and other virtues as the path;
however, because worldly people mostly take up the precepts,
the grasping for precepts (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is mentioned specifically.
In reality, it should be called "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"In this context, 'clinging' (parāmarśa) alone is used, omitting 'precepts and observances'."
Doubt regarding the truth is what is called "vicikitsā" (skeptical doubt). Now,
these five types [of hindrances]...
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
they are called "five lower" because they possess four lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The first is the lower realm (*dhātu-avara*).
Second, inferiority of result;
third, inferiority of person;
fourth, inferiority of what is obstructed.
Regarding the phrase "lower realms":
greed and hatred exist only within the desire realm.
Because those in the two upper realms do not possess what is called "lower" [affliction],
the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"Lust and anger..."
They do not transcend the desire realm.
Regarding the statement that "the fruits are inferior":
greed, hatred, and the attachment to precepts and rituals can bring about the inferior and obscuring fruits of the three miserable realms.
Therefore it is called "inferior fruit.
Thus the *Tattvasiddhi* says:
"Lust and hatred..."
It is said that one is born in the evil realms;
the same applies to the clinging to precepts and rituals,
such as observing the "ox-vow."
If it succeeds, one becomes an ox;
if one maintains it without success,
one gives rise to false views.
Denying cause and effect,
one is born in hell among the ranks of crows, chickens, and dogs.
It is also like this.
What are called the "lower fetters" of human beings are namely:
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā).
It arises only in ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and not in noble ones (ārya);
therefore, it is called "below humans.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
This view of a self-identity, adherence to precepts and rituals,
and doubt do not go beyond the stage of an ordinary person; as for those that are inferior, they are what is obstructed.
That is to say, these— personality view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—
are able to obstruct the first fruit;
thus they are called the "lower [stages] that are obstructed."
Question: All ten proclivities (anuśaya) obstruct the first fruit [of the path].
For what reason is this so?
Is this merely a partial explanation regarding these three obstacles for those in the first fruit?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because these three are heavy."
Therefore, it is explained in this partial manner.
For example, in the world, when a king comes or goes, he receives the name "king";
that case is also like this.
Furthermore, among the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*):
these six proclivities obstruct only the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
At the time of entering the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), [they are abandoned].
Both name and substance are exhausted.
Greed, anger, delusion, and pride collectively obstruct both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Because they obstruct the path of penetration,
although they are partially eliminated when entering the path of seeing.
Because they are not yet exhausted,
they are not designated as "abandoned.
Among the six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) previously mentioned as abandoned:
The three fetters (saṃyojana) are the root;
all others follow the body-view (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which is the root,
while the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) follows it.
Because one clings to permanence and annihilation based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is primary, while the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is secondary.
Because one relies on the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) to give rise to that grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) as supreme;
furthermore, doubt (vicikitsā) is the root,
while false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) is its consequence.
Because wrong views arise from a doubting mind,
we shall now address the fundamental point:

it is specifically stated that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are what obstruct the first fruit of the path.
The others all follow suit; therefore,
they are not discussed separately,
because those three bases subsume the three followers.
It is unnecessary to state separately that the two views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) constitute the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
[The opponent] asks:
Why are delusion (*moha*) and pride (*māna*) not stated to be the lower fetters?
Because those four aforementioned [factors] are absent below that level, it is established as such.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*; however, if one follows the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), it is as follows.
That which is correctly possessed of two lower [factors] is called a "lower fetter" (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
One is the lower realm (dhātu).
Greed and hatred exist only in the desire realm.
The other two— namely, the view of a self-identity, adherence to precepts and rituals, and doubt— are found in both humans and the lower realms.
It arises only in ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*);
such is the exact meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*).
As for its fruit being inferior:
Although this is not explicitly stated in the treatise,
it is logically unobjectionable when inferred according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Regarding those who are obstructed and inferior,
they are entirely dissimilar. Why is this so?
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it is taught that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are obstacles to the first fruit; therefore,
these must be established as being below that which is obstructed.
In the Abhidharma system,
the specific hindrances posed by these three fetters are not fixed.
The obstruction of precepts regarding the first fruit is that which is abandoned by one who proceeds step-by-step (anupūrvika).
The obstruction of precepts regarding the second fruit is as follows.
That which transcends what is abandoned by the Sakṛdāgāmin obstructs three fruits;
that which transcends what is abandoned by the Anāgāmin [obstructs the remaining fruits].
For this reason,
there are no obstructions regarding the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
This has been briefly indicated. 41.
The Meaning of the Five Higher Fetters (Part 5 of 5). Regarding the meaning of the five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it is as stated in the Sūtra:
First is ignorance;
second is arrogance;
third is restlessness.
The fourth is attachment to the realm of form;
the fifth is attachment to the formless realm.
These constitute a mind shrouded in the darkness of delusion.
That which is called ignorance;
that which exalts oneself and looks down upon others is termed pride.
A restless state of mind is called restlessness (auddhatya).
It is craving for the realm of form (rūpadhātu-rāga).
Attachment to one's own physical body is called "stain of form";
it refers to the affliction of craving within the formless realm.
Attachment to one's own mind is called "stain of the formless.
Now, among these five:
Possessing three kinds of "superiority," it is called the superior fetter (*ūrdhvabandhana*).
The first is superiority of realm (*dhātūrdhvatā*).
Second, superiority of person;
third, superiority of what is obstructed.
Regarding "superiority of realm":
These five types all exist within the two upper realms; because they arise there,
they are called "above the realms" (dhātu-upari).
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"Some say that those [beings] in the form and formless realms..."
They are called the "higher fetters" because they pertain to liberation.
As for the term "those above humans," it refers to these five types.
All of these arise from the practitioner;
therefore, they are called "superior to humans.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* says:
Since these five are all practiced by those in training (śaikṣa),
they are called "higher fetters" (ūrdhvabandhana).
That which is obstructed by them is the higher [realm].
These five types are collectively able to obstruct the higher fruit of arhatship; therefore,
they are called "higher fetters" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
If categorized separately,
the defilements of the form and formless realms, along with their associated restlessness,
are called "higher fetters" (ūrdhvabhāgīya) because they arise within the higher realms.
Question: Restlessness and frivolity also arise in the desire realm.
For what reason are they specifically taught as fetters only with respect to the higher realms?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains, saying:
"Within the two upper realms,
there are no coarse afflictions."
Because restlessness and frivolity are clearly manifest,
they are specifically mentioned;
[so too are] ignorance and pride.
These two types arise in those in training;
because they are superior to ordinary persons.
This is called the "higher fetter" (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana). Question:
Delusion and pride arise universally among both ordinary persons and noble ones.
Why is it that [the text] speaks exclusively of their arising in those in training (*śaikṣa*)?
The explanation states:
In reality, they arise in both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
However, for now, we shall take those arising in trainees (śaikṣa) as the "higher fetters" (ūrdhvabhāgīya).
If that is so, since greed and hatred arise in both ordinary persons and noble ones (ārya),
why do you not also take those arising in noble ones as higher fetters?
In the Sūtra, it is stated that sensual desire and ill will constitute the lower fetters.
The same principle should apply to equanimity; however,
at present, greed and hatred are bound to the lower realms.
The characteristics are distinct;
therefore, it is classified as an inferior fetter (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana) based on its belonging to the lower realm.
Having thus classified it as an inferior fetter.
It is not appropriate to further explain that the arising of a noble one constitutes the "superior bond.
If one discusses the obstruction to the fruit,
it does not differ from the previous explanation.
These five types are collectively able to obstruct the higher fruit of arhatship; therefore,
they are called "higher fetters" (ūrdhva-bandhana).
Question:
The lower fetters can obstruct the lower fruits;
what about the five higher fetters?
What serves as an obstruction to the higher fruits and the two intermediate fruits?
The commentary states:
Among those five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bandhanāni*),
there are two fetters, namely greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*pratigha*).
Those arising from the lower realm are designated as "lower fetters.
If one discusses their obstruction of the fruits,
they generally obstruct both of those two intermediate fruits.
The five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
This is a brief summary. 42.
The Meaning of the Five Kinds of Stinginess (Part Five): Regarding the meaning of the five kinds of stinginess.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
being firmly attached and unwilling to relinquish is designated as stinginess (*mātsarya*).
Avarice is divided into five types according to the distinction of its objects:
first, avarice regarding one's dwelling;
second, avarice regarding one's family.
Third is stinginess regarding giving;
fourth is stinginess regarding praise;
fifth is stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Regarding stinginess regarding one's dwelling:
there is a person who develops stinginess toward their own residence and thinks,
"I alone shall dwell here."
"Not allowing others to use [it],
but wishing for myself to have exclusive control—
this is the fault of stinginess."
There are five kinds in total.
First, one does not wish for future virtuous bhikṣus to come.
Second, they harbor anger and displeasure toward virtuous bhikṣus who have already arrived;
third, they desire to make them depart.
Fourth, they are unwilling to give them the property belonging to the Saṃgha.
Fifth, they conceive the notion of "mine" regarding items donated to the Saṃgha,
calculating it as a personal favor or debt of gratitude.
These are the five faults.
Such a person will be unable to relinquish those things held in common with others.
How much more so for all other things belonging to oneself?
Because of these faults,
regarding liberation...
Ultimately, there is no such division.
Regarding what is called "household stinginess":
there is a person who frequents the homes of worldly families.
Giving rise to a mind of stinginess,
they form this thought:
"In this household, I..."
He always enters and exits alone,
not employing others; even if there are others present, [he does so by himself].
To cause me to be most excellent—
this is the fault of stinginess.
It also has five kinds.
First, when laypeople encounter inauspicious events,
one shares their sorrow with them.
Second, when laypeople have matters of benefit,
one rejoices together with them.
Third, it cuts off the superior merit performed by laypeople;
fourth, it prevents the recipient from obtaining alms;
fifth, one will be reborn in that family as a ghost in a latrine or in other evil realms.
Regarding "generosity toward stinginess":
there are those who give rise to a mind of parsimony and attachment toward the objects they are giving.
They form this thought:
"May I alone receive these offerings here, while others receive nothing;
even if they were to give them, may it be so."
"Do not let it pass me by"—
this is the fault of stinginess,
which likewise has five aspects.
First, one will constantly lack the necessities of life;
second, it prevents the donor from gaining merit;
third, it prevents the recipient from obtaining wealth and benefit.
Fourth, disparaging virtuous people;
fifth, having a mind that is constantly troubled by anxiety.
Because of these faults, [one falls].
Such a person will be reborn in hell in the future;
even if they should obtain human form,
they will always remain in poverty, possessing no wealth or resources.
Praising the Miserly:
There are those who, when others offer praise,
give rise to a mind of stinginess and envy.
To think thus:
"May I alone be praised; do not praise others; let no one surpass me"—this is stinginess regarding reputation and praise (*yaśaḥ-śloka-mātsarya*).
These are the five kinds of faults of stinginess.
The first is hearing praise of others.
First, the mind is constantly agitated;
second, one reviles virtuous people;
third, one exalts oneself and disparages others.
Fourth, one will constantly suffer an evil reputation.
Fifth, throughout hundreds of thousands of future lifetimes,
one will never possess a pure mind.
Regarding what is called "miserliness regarding the Dharma":
there are those who give rise to a mind of stinginess toward the Dharma and then think as follows:
May I alone know the twelve divisions of the scriptures and not allow others to know them;
even if others should know them, may they not surpass me.
Furthermore, may I understand their meaning for myself.
To keep it secret and not explain it constitutes a fault of distinction;
there are seven such types.
First, one is born blind throughout one's life;
second, one is constantly dull-witted and ignorant;
third, one is born amidst many enemies and lacks self-mastery.
Fourth, they fall away from the noble embryo;
fifth, they are enemies and thieves to all Buddhas;
sixth, they are shunned by virtuous people.
There are seven things that no evil-doer fails to commit.
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the five types of stinginess.
43. The Meaning of the Five Moments of Mind (Part 5). Regarding the meaning of the five moments of mind, as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:
"Moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the momentary disintegration [of conditioned phenomena].
The sin of doubt and slander arises within the mind;
because it is like a sprout produced from a poisonous seed in the world, it is called a "mental sprout" (citta-śalya).
There are five kinds of doubt:
first, doubt regarding the Buddha;
second, doubt regarding the Dharma.
Third, doubting the precepts;
fourth, doubting the methods of teaching and transformation;
fifth, slandering and piercing virtuous people.
Regarding those who doubt the Buddha:
there are some whose minds lack correct faith toward the Buddha,
and they form such thoughts as these.
To act as a great deceiver toward the Buddha and as a great deceiver toward the Great Teacher is what is meant by "doubting the Dharma."
There are some who do not have right faith in the Dharma and think to themselves:
"The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are false."
It is because what is taught by the non-Buddhists is false.
Regarding doubt concerning the precepts:
there are those whose minds lack right faith toward the precepts.
They form this thought:
"Is the Dharma of the precepts taught by the Buddha superior,
or is the 'cow-precept' and so forth taught by the non-Buddhists superior?"
Regarding those who doubt the teaching:
there are some who do not have correct faith in the gates of the five perfections and so forth.
One should form this thought:
"These five perfections and so forth truly enable a person to attain nirvana."
It should not be done. Regarding those who speak slanderously and with malice:
suppose there is someone toward a virtuous bhikṣu.
Being slandered and attacked crosswise makes one appear frivolous and shallow;
this is the first of the five [faults].
The middle three gates contradict the veneration of the Buddha;
they contradict the veneration of the Dharma.
The latter gate contradicts the principle of the five mental states of reverence for the Sangha.
This is a brief summary. 44.
The Meaning of the Five Mental Bonds (Part Five). Regarding the meaning of the five mental bonds, as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: the five mental bonds are as follows.
Afflictions and unwholesome dharmas entangle the mind and are not relinquished; therefore,
it is called "bondage of the mind."
The bonds of the mind differ;
briefly stated, there are five kinds.
The first is attachment to one's own body.
Second, craving for the five external sense-pleasures;
third, delighting in association with householders and those who have gone forth;
fourth, having no joy or pleasure in the noble speech.
Fifth, regarding wholesome dharmas,
one considers a small attainment to be sufficient.
These are the five fetters.

45. The Meaning of the Six Defilements (Part Five, End): The Meaning of the Six Defilements, Analyzed through Seven Gates. Listing the Names and Providing Explanations: 1. Distinguishing their differences by correlating them with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). 2. Distinguishing their bases by correlating them with the ten latent dispositions. 3. Analysis according to the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). 4. Analysis according to the realms (*dhātu*). 5. Analysis according to the natures (*svabhāva*). 6. Analysis according to the paths (*mārga*). 7. First, listing the names.
The explanation of their characteristics and the meaning of the six impurities are as described in the Abhidharma.
What are called malice, resentment, deceit, arrogance, guile,
and affliction: these constitute the intent to harm toward all sentient beings.
To call this "harm" means that resentment and enmity are not relinquished;
to designate it as "hatred" means that it is held fast.
Deception is termed *māyā* (fraud);
self-exaltation is called *mada* (arrogance);
and crookedness is designated as *śāṭhya* (sycophancy).
Tormenting anxiety is called *nīvaraṇa* (affliction).
These six are all able to defile the pure mind;
thus they are termed "impurities" (*mala*). This concludes this section.
Next, the distinctions among the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are clarified.
As stated in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*:
"Among the afflictions (*kleśa*), the root is predominant."
It is said that they act as messengers;
the moisture they produce is called the defilement of entanglement (paryavasthāna).
Therefore, it is said in a parable:
It is like a jar filled with ghee from which the liquid flows out;
the ghee contained therein is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The secretions that emerge are a metaphor for the defilements of the enveloping fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Within these knots from which the secretions arise, [the following is explained].
The meaning of binding tightly is explained as being "envelopments" (paryavasthāna);
the meaning of light binding is...
It is described as a defilement,
as in the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
Thus ends the commentary on these two gateways.
Next, in contrast to the ten proclivities (*daśānuśaya*), their specific bases are clarified as explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*:
the two defilements of malice (*vyāpāda*) and resentment (*upanāha*).
It arises based on hatred;
because of the latent tendency of hatred,
one desires to harm the other.
Furthermore, due to anger,
one harbors resentment and does not let it go;
these are two defilements that cause deception and arrogance.
Covetousness arises;
because of the underlying tendency of covetousness,
one deceives the person before them.
They seize their wealth and profit;
furthermore, because of greed,
they become arrogant upon gaining profit.
Furthermore, because of greed,
one becomes attached to one's own body and consequently develops a sense of self-importance.
The defilement of flattery arises based on the five views;
for those who are not clever and sharp-witted are incapable of being flattering.
The defilement of vexation arises based on the grasping of views;
for one who grasps at views considers what is inferior to be superior,
yet seeks that superiority and does not obtain it.
Because they give rise to affliction,
the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Harmfulness and resentment depend upon hatred."
Deceit and arrogance depend upon greed;
that is to say, they arise from the basis of the five false views and sycophancy.
It is said that the fruit of the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is affliction (*daurmanasya*).
One should know that these three gates are now concluded.
Next, we shall proceed to analyze consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses.
These six defilements arise in the mental ground (manobhūmi).
It does not extend to the five consciousnesses;
the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Tattvasiddhi* follow this same explanation. These four gates are now concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish them according to the realms (*dhātu*).
The realms refer to the three realms.
Among the six defilements (*mala*), [the following...]
Malice, resentment, and vexation are of the nature of hatred;
they exist only in the desire realm.
Regarding flattery (*śāṭhya*) and deception (*māyā*):
because flattery exists as far as the highest limit of the first dhyāna,
the Brahmā King of the first dhyāna [possesses it].
Deceiving the assembly of Brahmās with flattery,
he said, "I am the most supreme;
do not go to the Buddha's dwelling."
Furthermore, out of deceit,
the bhikṣu Kālakarṇī went there to challenge and interrogate him.
He remained silent and did not respond.
Grasping Kṛṣṇadanta by the hand,
he searched for him in a secluded place.
It reaches as high as the third dhyāna.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
although it may arise in the higher realms, [it does not extend further].
These belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
According to that school’s tenet, the afflictions (*kleśa*) can arise by taking recourse [to these objects]. Thus ends this section on the five gates.
Next, they are distinguished by way of their nature (*svabhāva*).
"Nature" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Among these six stains:
Malice, resentment,
and vexation are invariably unwholesome;
the remaining three are indeterminate.
Those belonging to the desire realm are exclusively unwholesome;
those belonging to the higher realms...
The tenets of the various schools differ.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it is likewise unwholesome.
According to the Abhidharma,
everything belonging to the higher realms is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This concludes the six gates.
Next, they are distinguished according to the path.
"Path" refers to the paths of seeing and cultivation.
These [six types] are as follows:
These are the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation;
they are severed by the path of cultivation because they arise in dependence upon specific objects.
The meaning of the six impurities, which does not pertain to the vision of the truths,
has been briefly explained in this manner.
46. The Meaning of the Seven Outflows (Part Five). Regarding the meaning of the seven outflows, it is explained in detail within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: [text follows].
The meaning of the seven outflows (*āsrava*) is as explained in the *Saptāsrava-sūtra*;
it should be understood according to that *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
All afflictions flow and pour forth without ceasing,
just like a festering sore.
Therefore, they are called "outflows" (āsrava).
These outflows differ from one another;
in a single category, seven are taught.
What are these seven names?
First is the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*);
second is the outflow of cultivation (*bhāvanā-āsrava*).
Third, the outflow of the sense faculties;
fourth, the outflow of evil;
fifth, the outflow of intimacy.
Sixth is the outflow of sensation (vedanā-āsrava).
Seventh is the outflow of mindfulness (smṛti-āsrava).
As for what is called the outflow of views (dṛṣṭi-āsrava):
This name is derived from that which is obstructed; namely,
the afflictions of views and doubt,
which are able to obstruct the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, it is called the "outflow of views" (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*). As for the term "outflow of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-āsrava*),
this too is named after that which is obstructed.
The three outflows (*āsrava*) are afflictions that can obstruct the path of cultivation; therefore,
they are called "outflows of cultivation."
Regarding the "faculties" (indriya) and "outflows" (āsrava),
as it is said in the Sūtras:
the eye, ear, nose, and so forth.
That which is capable of producing [defilements] is called a "root" (indriya). Because outflows (āsrava) arise in dependence upon these roots,
they are termed "roots of outflow."
Regarding what are called "evil outflows":
these refer to all evil elephants, evil kings, evil nations, evil associates, and so forth,
which are capable of harming people.
It is described as evil;
because evil can give rise to outflows (*āsrava*),
it is called "evil outflow" (*pāpāsrava*).
Regarding those things that lead to outflows:
clothing, food and drink, lodgings, and medicine—
these four requisites.
When outflows arise from what is proximate,
they are called "outflows through proximity.
As for what are called "outflows through feeling":
Because the perception of feeling can give rise to various outflows (*āsrava*),
it is called the "outflow of feeling.

Regarding the fetter of delusion (*moha-saṃyojana*):
it refers to being unable to comprehend an object when taking it as a cognitive condition.
Therefore, it is called delusion (*moha*).
This is still the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of delusion;
although their general characteristics are the same, [they differ in specific application].
There is a difference in their breadth and narrowness:
the latent tendency of delusion (moha-anuśaya) is broad,
whereas the fetter of delusion (moha-saṃyojana) is narrow.
Among the latent tendencies of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*),
there are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*):
the first is the non-common [ignorance].
Second is association.
Regarding what is called "unshared," it refers to being unable to comprehend the conditions regarding both principle and phenomena.
It is called "unshared" (āveṇika) because it does not arise simultaneously with any afflictions.
As for the term "associated" (saṃprayukta):
Excluding the aforementioned unshared [afflictions], among all other afflictions,
there is the mind of *śāṭhya* (deceit).
This is called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).
This refers exclusively to unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*),
in order to include the fetter of delusion (*moha-saṃyojana*).
Why is this so? Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),
it is necessary to select and establish that which involves mental attention (*manasikāra*).
This is considered a fetter (*saṃyojana*).
Because that which stands alone possesses firm and powerful strength,
the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
It is an independent affliction included among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding what is called the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*):
To exalt oneself while disparaging others is called pride (*māna*);
this is still the underlying tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*).
Regarding the fetter of doubt:
it is the state of hesitation and indecision concerning the True Path.
Therefore, it is called doubt (*vicikitsā*).
This is equivalent to the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
As for what is called the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*):
The "adjacent wrong views" (sīlavrataparāmarśa) and these three types of inverted seeking are called "views" (dṛṣṭi).
These are precisely the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
Regarding the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*):
these are the two types of grasping— grasping at precepts and views—
which grasp and cling to their respective objects.
Therefore, it is called the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
This is equivalent to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Question:
For what reason are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) combined into the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*),
while the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) are combined into the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*)?
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* explains:
Because of the equality of names and so forth,
and because of the equality of entities and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "equality of names and so forth":
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vyākhyā* states:
"The views of self, extremes,
and wrong views are the names of its daughters."
The two types of grasping— grasping at precepts and views—
are the names for males;
since male and female are relative designations, they are referred to as "names" and so forth.
For what reason are the three views said to be "female"?
A female is an intimate person; these [three] are the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
The parents were deluded regarding the principle;
since the meaning resided within,
they followed that which was deluded and, by way of metaphor, designated it as "female."
For what reason are the two types of grasping called "male"?
"Male" refers to the externalist;
the two types of grasping are grasping at precepts and views.
It arises following others;
it does not personally engage with the delusion regarding principle.
Its meaning lies in what is external.
Therefore, it is designated as "male" by means of its metaphorical designation;
such is the meaning of the name.
As for the phrase "the entity and so forth":
Because these are called the eighteen *anuśaya* (proclivities) by nature, they are said to be equal in substance.
What are the eighteen?
Within the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), there are six for each of the three realms.
Thus, there are eighteen.
Regarding the six of the desire realm:
these are the false views of the desire realm.
The pervasive delusions regarding the Four Noble Truths constitute four [afflictions]: namely,
the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes.
Belonging to delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering,
these constitute two [categories];
together with the previously mentioned [four], they total six.
Since there are six [realms] in the desire realm,
the same applies to the form and formless realms;
thus, there are eighteen.
Among the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*),
there are six for each of the three realms,
totaling eighteen.
Regarding the six [afflictions] of the desire realm:
the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) within the desire realm is universally deluded regarding the four truths.
These are thus taken as four.
The attachment to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is deluded regarding the two truths of suffering and the path;
these are thus taken as two.
Including the preceding [two], six are thus explained.
As it is with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
so too are the categories of the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*) the same.
Thus there are eighteen;
the matters are equal in this way,
as they possess these two meanings.
The three views are combined into one;
the two views are combined into one.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
It is not so. They say that the ten proclivities (daśa-ānuśaya) are simultaneously deluded regarding the four truths (catur-āryasatya).
It cannot be said that they are identical to the entities such as names and so forth;
rather, because the faults of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are particularly grave,
they are established separately as the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
How is the fault so grave? As stated in the "Chapter on the Nine Fetters" (*Navasaṃyojana-varga*) of the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the fault of clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is difficult to abandon.
People of the world mostly adopt this as their path,
failing to perceive its faults.
For example, just as those within our own tradition take discarded rags (pāṃśukūla) as the path and so forth,
while various non-Buddhists take their own practices as the path and so forth;
furthermore, this clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) contradicts the Eightfold Noble Path.
Because this exists,
although there is practice,
it is empty and nothing is attained.
Furthermore, it can cause one to experience suffering in two lifetimes;
for instance, by performing various ascetic practices such as the cow-vow or the chicken-vow,
one undergoes suffering in the present life.
One will fall into the evil realms and undergo suffering in future lives;
such is the attachment to precepts.
As for the fault of attachment to views:
One who clings to all false phenomena will not attain reality;
this should be known.
All of this is due to the power of the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Such are the faults;
because these faults exist, [it is so].
These are called the fetters of grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*),
not by virtue of names and so forth.
As for the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*):
To be stingy and unwilling to relinquish one's own body or wealth is therefore called "miserliness" (mātsarya).
Regarding the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*):
it is called envy because one resents others who excel oneself.
These two are none other than the fetters of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
Why, among the envelopments, are only these two designated as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*)?
The treatise itself explains:
Because stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) arise independently and apart from the other two [groups],
they arise by their own power alone among the eight or nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Because it does not combine with others, it is called "standing alone. Question: [Why is this so?]
Within all afflictions,
there are always ignorance, torpor, restlessness, and so forth;
why then do you say it is "alone"?
The commentary states:
There is a reason for this;
it is because of the sleep and agitation of ignorance.
It exists in all places;
as this and that are darkly interconnected,
words fail and are not discussed.
Apart from this,
it does not arise together with any of the latent tendencies (anuśaya);
therefore, it is called "standing alone."
These two, stinginess and envy, are said to be exclusively unwholesome;
they are neither wholesome nor indeterminate.
Therefore, it is said that one should "abandon these two."
Why are only those that are independent taken as fetters?
This has been explained above:
because they are independent afflictions.
Because their power is firm and strong,
and their binding is secure,
they are called fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, the preceding seven fetters are each independent;
now, for the sake of conforming to them,
[the following are treated similarly].
Why is it that only those independent [defilements] are taken, and why are only those defilements dissociated from the two [realms] taken as fetters,
rather than the unwholesome defilements?
Its power is potent and its bonds are firm; for this reason,
it is specifically grasped.
If this is the case,
then among the aforementioned seven fetters, the two views of self-identity and extremes are exclusively indeterminate.
All afflictions within the two upper realms are also indeterminate (avyākṛta) and are not of an unwholesome nature (akuśala).
Why is it called a "fetter" (saṃyojana)?
The explanation states:
the first seven are of the nature of latent proclivities (anuśaya).
Because their nature is firm and strong,
even those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) can still bind; therefore,
they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
The others are not of the nature of proclivities (*anuśaya*); their power is slight.
Furthermore, they must be unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Only then can it form a bond;
it is not like the preceding seven.
Since it exists here [in this state], [it functions differently].
The *Śāstra* asks:
"For what reason are *styāna* (sloth) and *auddhatya* (restlessness) not considered *saṃyojana* (fetters)?
The treatise itself explains: [as follows].
When sleep occurs together with the two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and various fetters (*saṃyojana*),
it is not termed "independent.
Furthermore, it is categorized as either unwholesome (*akuśala*), defiled-neutral (*kliṣṭāvyākṛta*), or non-defiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*).
It is not called "separation from the two.
For this reason, one does not grasp.
Again, he asked:
Why is the fetter of torpor (*styāna-nivaraṇa*) not considered a tie (*saṃyojana*)?
The treatise itself explains:
"Torpor is associated with all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)."
Therefore, it is not independent;
since sleep permeates all three natures,
it is not separate from the two.
For this reason, they are not grasped.
Why are shamelessness and lack of dread not considered fetters?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
although shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) are distinct from these two [roots], they are nonetheless included within them.
Yet it does not exist independently;
therefore, it is not a fetter.
This is the absence of shame and lack of remorse.
It is associated exclusively with unwholesome states of the desire realm;
therefore, it is called "separated from two.
For what reason is the fetter of remorse (*kaukṛtya-saṃyojana*) not designated as a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*)?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
Although regret exists independently,
it is not separate from these two.
Therefore, it is not a fetter,
because remorse exists within both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Regarding the two envelopments of anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*),
why are they not considered fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
The treatise itself explains:
Although anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are independent,
they are nonetheless distinct from the other two;
this is because some maintain that these possess the nature of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, they are not mentioned [among the primary afflictions].
Anger is of the nature of hatred;
concealment is of the nature of greed.
According to those who speak thus,
only eight envelopments (paryavasthāna) are established;
[as stated] in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*.
The same applies to this statement.
Question: For what reason are the six stains (*mala*) not considered fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"The tightly bound afflictions are called *paryavasthāna* (entanglements)."
The light fetters of affliction are said to be "impurities" among the tight bonds.
If one does not even accept a slight offense,
how much less so a minor fetter?
Therefore, it is not so stated.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
however, it is not thus.
What does he say?
The two entanglements of stinginess and envy are base afflictions.
Therefore, they are called fetters;
there is no other meaning.
What is meant by "corrupt"?
The commentary on that treatise states:
"Because of stinginess, one is greedily attached to one's body and wealth;
thus, even though one sees the suffering of poverty,"
They have no intention to rescue or deliver others because they harbor envy; due to this jealousy,
they resent others gaining benefit.
Furthermore, one is submerged by greed and anger, which constitute the greatest transgressions.
Anger leads to rebirth in the evil realms;
it is primarily due to greed and anger that this occurs.
Because of these faults,
stinginess arises from greed,
and envy is distinguished from hatred.
Furthermore, stinginess and envy are prevalent among devas and humans who are prone to parsimony; therefore,
they are specifically mentioned here.
The others are not thus;
they are omitted and not explained.
The nine fetters are likewise.
Question:
Is there any dharma associated with views that is bound by the fetter of craving but not bound by the fetter of views, yet is still said to be driven by the latent tendency of views?
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"It exists;
that is to say, when the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*) has already arisen within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)."
When the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
at that time, regarding the truths of cessation and the path, there are the two types of grasping:
grasping after rules and observances and grasping after views.
The associated mental states and non-mental states, such as arising, abiding, and ceasing,
are bound by the fetter of craving belonging to the lower realms of cessation and the path;
for craving conditions the arising of that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
It is not the fetter of views;
rather, all wrong views pertaining to the truths of cessation and the path arise by directly taking principle as their object.
They do not take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object;
therefore, they cannot bind this dharma.
Under the Truths of Suffering and Origin, there are eleven universal latent proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Because they have already been abandoned, one is no longer bound by them;
therefore, this is not called being bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana).
Nevertheless, one is simultaneously bound by the two graspings: grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) and grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
They are called "proclivities of views" (dṛṣṭy-ānuśaya) because they are bound by [the proclivity of] views.
This is precisely because, among the nine fetters (nava-saṃyojana), the two types of grasping (dvaya-parāmarśa) are not classified as the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana).
It is not called the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Among the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*),
that which is named the proclivity of views is called the proclivity of views.
This is a rough explanation of the nine fetters (*navasaṃyojana*).
